inputs.need:
I am an epidemiologist in the clinical research unit of a university hospital. We run the regional pneumonia registry, which has enrolled every adult admitted with community-acquired pneumonia to the four hospitals in our region since 2016, with severity scores, microbiology and treatment. I want to use it for a registry-based cohort study of what happens to patients in the five years after discharge: death, new cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction, stroke, admission for heart failure), readmission for pneumonia, and loss of independence, meaning a move into a care home. Clinicians keep saying that pneumonia ages people and that the cardiovascular risk stays high for years, but most of what I have seen covers only the first 30 or 90 days.

The registry can be linked to the national death register and to hospital admissions across the region, and the regional statistics office can provide a comparison group from the general population matched on age, sex and area. Linkage needs approval from the registry's data access committee and from the statistics office, and the committee has told us it will not decide before its February meeting at the earliest.

I need help framing the question, choosing the comparison group (the general population, or patients admitted with other acute infections), handling confounding by existing heart disease and frailty, and defining the time windows. I also need to know what published evidence exists, because a colleague keeps quoting a doubling of cardiovascular risk over ten years that I cannot trace. The registry holds about 11,800 patients discharged alive between 2016 and 2021, so five years of follow-up are complete for all of them.
inputs.constraints: Secondary use of registry and linked data only; no patient contact; one epidemiologist and a part-time statistician for twelve months; linkage requires the data access committee's and the statistics office's approval.

response.title: Five-year outcomes after community-acquired pneumonia in a regional registry cohort
response.subtitle: Registry-based cohort with two comparison groups and linked outcomes
response.statement: A regional registry holds 11,800 adults discharged alive after community-acquired pneumonia between 2016 and 2021, with five years of possible follow-up. Clinicians believe that pneumonia raises cardiovascular risk and loss of independence for years, but local evidence covers only the first months and a widely quoted ten-year doubling of cardiovascular risk has no traceable source. A registry-based cohort with linked outcomes and a carefully chosen comparison group can estimate the long-term excess risk, provided that frailty and existing heart disease are handled.
response.whoAffected: Adults who survive a pneumonia admission, especially older people with heart disease or frailty; their families; hospital and primary care clinicians planning follow-up.
response.whatHurts: If the excess cardiovascular risk persists, survivors are missing follow-up that could prevent events; if it does not, clinicians are worrying patients with an untraced figure.
response.currentPractice: Follow-up after pneumonia ends at discharge or one clinic visit; no routine cardiovascular review; no local data beyond 90 days.
response.whyNow: Five years of follow-up are complete for every registry patient discharged by 2021, and linkage requests can be decided in February 2027.
response.constraints: Secondary use of registry and linked data only; no patient contact; one epidemiologist and a part-time statistician for twelve months; linkage requires the data access committee's and the statistics office's approval.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Pneumonia survivors receive follow-up proportionate to their real long-term risk and stay independent for as long as possible.
response.summary: Problem framed as a registry-based cohort study of five-year outcomes with confounding by frailty as the main threat.

records.title: Cardiovascular events in the five years after hospitalisation for community-acquired pneumonia: a linked national cohort of 18,400 adults with matched controls
records.authors: Lindqvist-Opoku S, Marchetti-Hale D, Tanaka-Boateng R
records.abstract: We followed 18,400 adults discharged after community-acquired pneumonia and 73,600 population controls matched on age, sex and area for five years using linked national data. The hazard ratio for a first myocardial infarction, stroke or heart failure admission was 1.9 in the first year and 1.3 in years two to five. Adjustment for cardiovascular disease and diabetes before the pneumonia reduced the later estimate to 1.15 (95 percent CI 1.07 to 1.24). Mortality was higher throughout. The authors note that frailty was not measured and that population controls were healthier than patients in ways the adjustment could not capture.

records.title: Long-term mortality after community-acquired pneumonia compared with other acute infections: a registry study
records.abstract: Using a hospital infection registry, we compared five-year mortality of 6,200 adults discharged after community-acquired pneumonia with 9,100 adults discharged after urinary tract infection or cellulitis. Five-year mortality was 38 percent after pneumonia and 33 percent after the other infections. After adjustment for age, comorbidity and a frailty score, the hazard ratio was 1.12 (95 percent CI 1.04 to 1.20). The excess was concentrated in the first year. The authors argue that part of the apparent long-term effect of pneumonia seen against the general population reflects the frailty of people who are admitted with any infection.

records.title: Choosing the comparison group in studies of outcomes after infection: general population versus hospitalised controls
records.abstract: We compared the two usual comparison groups for studies of long-term outcomes after an infection admission. General population controls overstate the effect of the infection because admitted patients are frailer and sicker before the infection. Controls admitted with another infection understate it when that infection shares some of the same long-term effects. In three linked datasets, estimates against the two comparison groups bracketed the estimate from an analysis using each patient's own history before the infection. We recommend reporting results against both comparison groups and measuring frailty before the index admission.

records.title: Frailty, pre-existing cardiovascular disease and long-term outcomes after pneumonia: a confounding analysis
records.abstract: In 9,600 adults discharged after pneumonia and matched population controls, we measured frailty with a hospital frailty score calculated from admissions in the two years before the pneumonia. Adjusting for this frailty score halved the excess five-year mortality, from a hazard ratio of 1.62 to 1.29, and reduced the excess of cardiovascular events from 1.34 to 1.14. Adjusting for complications during the pneumonia admission reduced the estimates further, but the authors warn that these complications lie on the causal path and should not be adjusted for in the main analysis.

records.title: Moving into long-term care within two years after hospitalisation for pneumonia in adults aged 75 and over
records.abstract: Among 4,300 adults aged 75 and over who lived at home before a pneumonia admission, 9 percent moved into long-term care within two years, against 4 percent of matched adults from the general population. The difference was largest among people with cognitive impairment and among those who lived alone. About half of the moves happened within three months of discharge. The authors suggest that loss of independence is a patient-important outcome that registries rarely capture and that care home entry can be identified from linked address and social care data.

records.title: Linking pneumonia registries to national death and hospital admission data: completeness and pitfalls
records.abstract: We linked a regional pneumonia registry to national death data and regional hospital admissions using deterministic and probabilistic methods. Linkage succeeded for 98.7 percent of registry patients. Causes of death on death certificates agreed with hospital diagnoses for cardiovascular deaths in 81 percent of cases. Admissions to hospitals outside the region were missed, affecting about 4 percent of patients who moved during follow-up. We recommend censoring at the date of leaving the region and using hospital diagnoses rather than death certificates alone to define cardiovascular events.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records from the broader second search, appraised at abstract level; the first, narrower search returned nothing. Against population controls, cardiovascular risk after pneumonia is raised most in the first year (hazard ratio 1.9) and less in years two to five (1.3), and adjustment for earlier cardiovascular disease and frailty shrinks the later excess to about 1.15. Against patients admitted with other infections, the mortality excess is small and concentrated in the first year. Methods work shows the two comparison groups bracket the truth. Care home entry doubles in older adults. Linkage is near complete. No retrieved record supports a ten-year doubling of cardiovascular risk.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent observational cohorts with serious confounding by frailty and comparison-group choice; estimates shrink with better adjustment. Low certainty that a long-term cardiovascular excess persists beyond the first year.

response.reading: Frailty and existing heart disease sit before both the pneumonia admission and later events, so the size of any long-term effect depends on how they are measured and which comparison group is used. The first year after discharge carries most of the excess, and later years much less. Loss of independence is the outcome patients notice and registries rarely record. Everything rests on linkage that is not yet approved.

Clinicians keep saying that pneumonia ages people and that the cardiovascular risk stays high for years, but most of what I have seen covers only the first 30 or 90 days.

The registry can be linked to the national death register and to hospital admissions across the region, and the regional statistics office can provide a comparison group from the general population matched on age, sex and area. Linkage needs approval from the registry's data access committee and from the statistics office, and the committee has told us it will not decide before its February meeting at the earliest.

I need help framing the question, choosing the comparison group (the general population, or patients admitted with other acute infections), handling confounding by existing heart disease and frailty, and defining the time windows. I also need to know what published evidence exists, because a colleague keeps quoting a doubling of cardiovascular risk over ten years that I cannot trace. The registry holds about 11,800 patients discharged alive between 2016 and 2021, so five years of follow-up are complete for all of them.
